items.name: Lithium jump starter
items.need: A dead battery is the most likely reason a car will not start when you need to leave, and there may be no second car around to jump from.
items.how_to_choose: Pick a lithium pack small enough to live in the glove compartment or door pocket; Popular Science's guide says most passenger cars start on about 400 to 600 amps, so huge numbers on the box matter little for a city car. Look for clamps with reverse-polarity protection and a UL 2743 mark on the unit itself, and treat any UL claim as the maker's until you see the mark. A jump starter only works if it is charged, so top it up every three months and after each use.

qty.note: One per car. Households without a car skip this item.

items.already_own: Jumper cables work only if another running car is nearby. An older jump pack is fine if it still holds a charge: charge it fully, leave it a week, and check that it still shows most of its charge.

items.name: Seatbelt cutter and window breaker
items.need: If a crash or flood jams the belts and the doors, a cutter and glass breaker within reach can get everyone out through a side window.
items.how_to_choose: AAA's tests found spring-loaded tools broke tempered side glass more reliably than hammer-style ones, and every tool cut a seat belt. No tool broke laminated glass, which many newer cars now use in side windows, so read the small label in the corner of each side window before you rely on one. Keep the tool fixed where the driver can reach it while belted in (key ring, visor or console), not loose in the glove compartment.

qty.note: One per car, reachable from the driver's seat. Households without a car skip this item.

items.already_own: Any spring-loaded punch-type tool with a guarded belt blade is good enough. Test the punch on a block of soft wood to see that it fires. If all your side windows are marked laminated, the tool is useful only for cutting belts.
items.tier_note: Two picks, the same tool single or as a pair: AAA found that no consumer tool breaks laminated glass and that the inexpensive spring-loaded kind did best on side windows, so a pricier one buys nothing the job needs.
items.research_note: empty_reason.cadillac was: Paying more buys no extra capability: AAA found no consumer tool breaks laminated glass, and the inexpensive spring-loaded type did best on tempered glass. The LifeHammer Safety Hammer Evolution (maker's page opened today; it states it does not work on laminated glass) is a larger mounted alternative, but its page showed no price and no second source was found. | item flag moved off the page 2026-11-16: AAA's published report does not name the brands it tested, so no pick here can claim to be one of the four tools that passed.

safety_notes.text: AAA tested six escape tools (three spring-loaded, three hammer-style). Four of the six broke tempered side glass and the spring-loaded type did better. None broke laminated glass. AAA says about 1 in 3 model-year 2018 vehicles had laminated side windows, so check the label in the bottom corner of each side window. AAA's steps: Stay calm, Unbuckle, Roll down or break a window, Exit. If the glass is laminated and the car is sinking, move to an air pocket, wait for the pressure to equalize, then open a door.

items.how_to_choose: Buy triangles that state they meet Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 125 (often marked DOT): that standard covers the reflective and fluorescent material and stability in wind. safety_notes.text: The federal standard for warning triangles is FMVSS No. 125 (49 CFR 571.125). It sets the shape (equilateral, sides 17 to 22 in), red reflective and orange fluorescent borders, a stand that holds up in a 40 mph wind, required maker marking (name, month and year, DOT symbol or a compliance statement) and illustrated set-up instructions. items.need: A child who can carry their own water, snack, light and comfort item frees an adult's hands on the stairs and gives the child a job.
items.how_to_choose: Choose by the child's height first: the maker sizes each pack to a body height, and its age labels are loose. As a guide, about ages 3 to 5 take a 5 to 8 liter pack, about 6 to 9 a 10 to 18 liter pack, and about 10 to 13 an 18 to 30 liter pack. These are sizes, not loads to reach: a child carries only what they can manage on your own stairs, and an adult keeps the water, medicines and contact details that matter. The loaded pack should never weigh more than 15% of the child's body weight, which is the American Academy of Pediatrics' ceiling for a school backpack (a 40 lb child: 6 lb at most), and lighter is better. Look for two padded shoulder straps and a chest strap so it stays on while walking down many flights of stairs.

items.name: Soft structured carrier for a baby or toddler
items.need: A stroller is useless on stairs; a carrier holds a baby against your chest, or a toddler on your back, and leaves both hands free for the rail.
items.how_to_choose: Match the carrier to the child you would be carrying now. Read the maker's age, weight and position limits, and try it on with that child and the adult who will wear it before you buy. A newborn needs a carrier its maker rates from birth; do not choose by the lower weight limit alone, because a carrier that lists 7 lb may still be recommended only from 3 months. A child aged 1 to 3 rides on your back, in a buckle-on soft structured carrier with a padded waist belt that is rated for the child's weight. An adult with a child on their back cannot also wear a backpack: wear the grab bag on your front, or have the second adult or the named helper carry it. With a baby on your front, the bag goes on your back. Every soft carrier sold in the US must meet the federal standard built on ASTM F2236. For any carrier, keep the face visible, the chin off the chest and the nose and mouth unobstructed, and check the child often. Practice each carry you would use, the back carry included, once on your own stairs, with the bag on, and keep one hand on the stair rail.

qty.note: One for each child who cannot walk a mile, in a carrier whose limits fit that child. One adult can wear one carrier, so two carried children need two adults or a named helper. Keep it with the grab bag, already adjusted to the adult most likely to wear it.

items.already_own: A carrier you already use and trust is the best one. Check that your child is within its age and weight limits now, that buckles and seams are sound, and that the model is not on CPSC's recall list. A carrier made for the first year does not cover a toddler: the BabyBjorn Baby Carrier Mini, for one, is rated by its maker for 0 to 12 months and 7 to 24 lb, with no back carry. A stretchy wrap works for small babies if you can tie it fast under stress.

safety_notes.text: The Academy's advice for babies, which this site applies to any child in any carrier: make sure you can always see the face, and that the nose and mouth are not blocked by fabric or by your body, and check often. Of slings it adds that the neck should be straight and the chin not pressed into the chest. It says babies born early or with breathing problems should not be put in backpacks or other upright carriers, because the position can make breathing harder. Check the seams and fasteners for rips and tears from time to time.
safety_notes.source_title: Baby Carriers: Backpacks, Front Packs & Slings

safety_notes.text: CPSC warns that babies under four months can suffocate in a carrier in two ways: fabric pressed against the nose and mouth, or a curled position with the chin on the chest that narrows the airway. Risk is higher for premature, low-birth-weight or unwell babies. Keep the face uncovered and visible at all times and check often.
safety_notes.source_title: Infant Deaths Prompt CPSC Warning About Sling Carriers for Babies (12 March 2010)

safety_notes.text: Soft infant and toddler carriers sold in the US must meet the mandatory federal standard, 16 CFR part 1226, which adopts ASTM F2236 (F2236-24 for products made after February 22, 2025). Slings are covered by a separate rule.
safety_notes.source_title: Soft Infant and Toddler Carriers Business Guidance

safety_notes.text: The International Hip Dysplasia Institute says short, occasional carrier use is unlikely to affect hip development, but for long periods of carrying, especially in the first six months, the hips should be able to spread apart with the thighs supported and the hips bent. Narrow-based carriers that do not support the thigh to the knee are not recommended for prolonged use.
safety_notes.source_title: Baby Carriers & Other Equipment

safety_notes.text: CDC's emergency list for families with infants includes ready-to-feed formula in single-serving bottles or cans for several days (checked monthly), at least one large pack of diapers, at least two packs of wipes, disposable cups, gallon-size resealable bags and a baby carrier. Bottles and nipples should not be used if they cannot be cleaned with safe water and soap.
safety_notes.source_title: Emergency List for Families With Infants and Young Children

items.name: Infant formula for the bag (formula-fed babies only)
items.need: If tap water is off or unsafe and there is no fridge, a formula-fed baby still needs every feed made safely; this is the formula and water to do it.
items.how_to_choose: Breastfeeding comes first: CDC calls it the safest way to feed an infant in a disaster, and this item is only for babies who already take formula. Pack the baby's own formula; this site never suggests changing it. If the baby's formula is sold ready-to-feed, pack that: it is sterile and needs no water. Choose the bottle size closest to one feed, because what is left after a feed is thrown away and an opened bottle cannot be kept without a fridge. If the baby's formula is sold only as powder, pack unopened powder, sealed bottled water measured for it, and a clean bottle or a disposable cup for each feed. Mix each feed fresh, with exactly the water and powder the label gives: measure the water first, add the powder with the container's scoop, close the lid and shake. Use it within 1 hour of starting the feed and throw away what is left. For a baby under 2 months, born early or with a weakened immune system, CDC says ready-to-feed is the safest choice: ask your pediatrician now what to pack. Check use-by dates every month and rotate stock into daily use.

qty.note: Count feeds, not fluid ounces: feeds in a normal day × days, for each formula-fed baby. With ready-to-feed, that is the number of bottles: buy the size closest to one feed (2 fl oz bottles for a baby who takes up to 2 fl oz, 8 fl oz bottles once the baby finishes most of one), and add a clean nipple or a disposable cup for each feed. Example: 8 feeds a day for 3 days is 24 bottles. With powder, pack unopened powder for that many feeds and enough sealed bottled water to mix each one to the label. By about 6 months most babies take 4 or 5 feeds a day. Feeds a day is the figure you give in the household setup; until you give one the site uses 8, which is this site's assumption and not medical advice.

safety_notes.text: Breastfeeding is the safest way to feed an infant in a disaster. For formula-fed infants, ready-to-feed formula is the safest choice in an emergency because it needs no added water and comes in sterile containers. Powdered formula needs safe water, a clean scoop and exact measuring; use mixed formula within 2 hours, or within 1 hour of the start of a feed, and throw away what is left.
safety_notes.source_title: Facts About Infant Feeding During Emergencies

safety_notes.text: Ready-to-feed formula is sterile and needs no added water; powdered formula is not sterile, so CDC says to use ready-to-feed for babies under 2 months, babies born early and babies with weakened immune systems. For powder, use bottled water until officials say the tap water is safe, use exactly the amounts on the label, measure the water first, add the powder with the scoop, close and shake. Use it within 1 hour of starting a feed and within 2 hours of making it, and throw away what is left. With no working fridge, make fresh formula for every feed. If you cannot wash a bottle and nipple with soap and safe water, use a disposable cup once and throw it away.
safety_notes.source_title: Prepare and Store Powdered Infant Formula in an Emergency
safety_notes.research_note: Opened by WebFetch 2026-11-16 (page last updated August 10, 2026). Source id cdc-infant-formula.

safety_notes.text: CDC's emergency list for families with infants includes ready-to-feed formula in single-serving bottles or cans for several days (checked monthly), at least one large pack of diapers, at least two packs of wipes, disposable cups, gallon-size resealable bags and a baby carrier. Bottles and nipples should not be used if they cannot be cleaned with safe water and soap.
safety_notes.source_title: Emergency List for Families With Infants and Young Children

safety_notes.text: On average a baby takes about 2.5 fl oz of formula per pound of body weight per day, usually no more than about 32 fl oz in 24 hours. Newborns take 1 to 2 fl oz a feed in the first week; by about 6 months, 6 to 8 fl oz at each of 4 or 5 feeds. Needs vary; ask your pediatrician.
safety_notes.source_title: Amount and Schedule of Baby Formula Feedings

safety_notes.text: FDA does not approve infant formula, but makers must notify FDA, follow sanitary controls and test for Salmonella and Cronobacter, and labels must carry preparation directions and a use-by date. FDA warns about formula imported or sold by third-party online sellers, which may not meet US requirements.
safety_notes.source_title: Infant Formula Homepage

safety_notes.text: All ByHeart Whole Nutrition powdered infant formula was recalled in November 2025 after an infant botulism outbreak (28 confirmed and 20 probable cases; declared over February 26, 2026). Do not use any ByHeart formula you still have.
safety_notes.source_title: Outbreak Investigation of Infant Botulism: Infant Formula (November 2025)

safety_notes.text: Nara Organics recalled all of its whole milk organic powdered infant formula in June 2026 after four infants developed botulism; the product was sold at Target and Nara.com. FDA declared that outbreak over on August 27, 2026. Neither this recall nor the ByHeart recall involves ready-to-feed liquid formula.
safety_notes.source_title: Outbreak Investigation of Infant Botulism: Powdered Infant Formula (June 2026)

safety_notes.text: Use prepared infant formula within 2 hours of preparing it and within 1 hour from when a feed begins. Throw away any formula left in the bottle after the feed. Formula that will not be used within 2 hours goes into a refrigerator at once and is used within 24 hours.
safety_notes.source_title: Infant Formula Preparation and Storage

safety_notes.text: CDC's page gives no separate time for an opened bottle of ready-to-feed formula, so follow the label. The maker of the example formula here says opened ready-to-use formula should not be kept at room temperature for longer than 2 hours, keeps in a refrigerator for up to 48 hours, and is thrown away one hour after a feed has begun or the bottle has been warmed; it also says never to dilute formula. Where a label and CDC differ, use the shorter time.
safety_notes.source_name: Enfamil (the maker's own instructions, not an official body)
safety_notes.source_title: How to Make Baby Formula: 3 Easy Steps for Safe Preparation

safety_notes.text: If you are told to evacuate, take your pets. Keep a lightweight evacuation kit: several days of food and water, medicines, a backup leash, collar and ID tag, a sturdy carrier for each pet, sanitation supplies, a photo of you with your pet, and something familiar. Microchip your pet and keep the registered phone number and address current. Know before an emergency where you could take your pet, and arrange with a neighbor, friend or relative to care for it or bring it out if you cannot.
safety_notes.source_title: Prepare Your Pets for Disasters

safety_notes.text: Keep a leash or carrier near the exit and keep pets in a carrier or on a leash during an emergency. Pets should wear a collar and tag with current contact details; microchipping, with the chip registered and kept up to date, is one of the best ways to be reunited. Write the pet's name and your phone numbers on the carrier and pack vaccination records.
safety_notes.source_title: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

safety_notes.text: The Center for Pet Safety is an independent non-profit that crash-tests pet carriers, crates and harnesses and lists the ones that pass on its CPS Certified page. A carrier or harness that is not on that list has not been shown to protect a pet in a crash.
safety_notes.source_title: CPS Certified

safety_notes.text: Never leave children, disabled adults or pets alone in a parked vehicle, even in winter. In a National Weather Service demonstration a car's interior passed 94 F in just over two minutes; opening the windows slightly does not meaningfully slow the heating, and deaths have happened on days in the 70s.
safety_notes.source_title: Children, Pets and Vehicles

items.name: Escape-resistant dog harness and leash
items.need: A scared dog can back out of a collar in seconds on a noisy street; a snug harness and a spare leash keep the dog attached to you. All three picks are dog harnesses: for a cat, the backup to the carrier is a harness made for cats.
items.how_to_choose: For a dog that slips harnesses, look for a design with a second strap behind the rib cage, and fit it so two fingers just slide under each strap. A cat belongs in its carrier during an evacuation; its backup is a harness made for cats, sized by the cat's chest, not one of the dog harnesses below.

items.name: Portable litter tray and litter (cats)
items.need: A cat shut in a carrier, a car or a shelter room for days still needs a litter box, and stress makes accidents more likely without one.
items.how_to_choose: For the bag, a fold-flat disposable cardboard tray is the lightest option and can be thrown away when you leave. Pack about three days of the litter your cat already uses in doubled zip bags (roughly 2 to 3 lb of clumping litter), a few waste bags and a scoop or spoon. Cats.com's tester found coated-cardboard trays work best with clumping clay litter and daily scooping.

qty.note: One tray per cat for a 3-day stay. Disposable trays are sold in packs of 4 or 5, so one pack covers most households. Dogs skip this item.

items.already_own: A disposable aluminum roasting pan or a shallow cardboard box lined with a trash bag works for a few days. What matters is that you have packed the cat's usual litter.

safety_notes.text: If you are told to evacuate, take your pets. Keep a lightweight evacuation kit: several days of food and water, medicines, a backup leash, collar and ID tag, a sturdy carrier for each pet, sanitation supplies, a photo of you with your pet, and something familiar. Microchip your pet and keep the registered phone number and address current. Know before an emergency where you could take your pet, and arrange with a neighbor, friend or relative to care for it or bring it out if you cannot.
safety_notes.source_title: Prepare Your Pets for Disasters

safety_notes.text: Keep a leash or carrier near the exit and keep pets in a carrier or on a leash during an emergency. Pets should wear a collar and tag with current contact details; microchipping, with the chip registered and kept up to date, is one of the best ways to be reunited. Write the pet's name and your phone numbers on the carrier and pack vaccination records.
